Three employers—HepcoMotion, Dormakaba, and Heathcoats—teamed up with Elmore AFC to host a charity football match that raised £1,063.07 for Hospiscare.
The event, held at Elmore’s grounds, featured 11-a-side teams and 15-minute games, promoting both teamwork and community spirit.
Organised by Dormakaba, Ryan Perry said: "To organise an event enjoyed by everyone who took part on behalf of such a wonderful charity is an honour. The work the hospice does is incredible, caring for people desperately in need and completely funded by donations. I'm glad the amazing community of businesses and the people of Tiverton could contribute and do our bit."
HepcoMotion’s Paul Mallinson added: “As one of the largest employers in Tiverton, we were pleased to join forces with other local employers. The funds raised will make a significant difference to the hospice, helping them continue their vital work in our community.”
Lauren Butt, representative of Hospiscare, said: “We would like to extend a huge thank you to Dormakaba, HepcoMotion, Heathcoats, and Elmore AFC for uniting for an incredible day of fundraising. Your support is crucial to our efforts, and we have never needed your help as much as we do right now. This contribution will go a long way in supporting our patients and their families.”
Plans are already underway for another charity match in 2025.

headline: Mint Quick Edit | Infosys GST bill defies logic
description:
Indian tax authorities apparently expected Infosys to pay GST on services availed by it from its overseas units, but since these went into exports, they would’ve anyway qualified for input tax credit. This muddle should never have arisen. Tax uncertainty is bad for business. content: Taxation should never be like reading tea leaves. But the storm in a teacup over a goods and services tax (GST) demand of about ₹32,400 crore made of Infosys (now being relooked) suggests a system full of riddles. As reported, services were availed by Infosys from its overseas branches.
By one interpretation of India’s GST rules, this would have required “reverse charge" tax payments on these imports by the company. Hence the tax bill. However, the services Infosys bought went into its software exports, which are tax-free and thus eligible for input tax credits.
So, if the company could anyway claim the tax back, why should it apply in the first place? A reverse charge mechanism does exist under GST. But its applicability in this case is unclear. On its part, Infosys has denied any evasion, arguing that GST simply isn’t applicable on stuff bought from its own foreign units.
The case is being examined by the Directorate General of GST Intelligence. Should some quirk or technicality mean it still owes money, then it’s the rules that would need sorting out. Such tax riddles create uncertainty for businesses. It would be best if tax authorities clarify what exactly the law says.
